you can achieve a maximum of 315% with melee prowess, enduring strike, and the dual effect mods. There are 3 slots open for status chance mods achieving a max status multiplier of 180%. The base status chance is 10%, so you get at most 28% status chance.

A specific mod gives 60% crit chance right off the bat (so 15*1.6 = 24) with 1 mod, you already have a higher chance of critting than 1 status mod proccing. I'm not going to include another mod because you really don't need it.

In statistics, the chance of critting via a naive RNG method has something similar to IID, independent and identically distributed random variables. That means every strike has its own random variable and doesn't affect the chance of future strikes critting/proccing. (assuming perfect RNG, which it isn't). This gives a specific playstyle an innate advantage.

Crit with this playstyle allows you to increase your attack speed every time you crit, meaning you'll be outputting more strikes. Each strike procs its own crit/status. Therefore, more strikes = higher overall chance (since chances are additive here). You can replace a status mod for this playstyle. (you have 15% chance per strike, high base speed = higher chance) replace the leftover status mod with a dual status mod.

You shouldn't depend on a specific mod in high levels because you'll want a different mod instead. Other players will be more likely to be selfish and pick what they need (e.g. certain characters would want more energy siphon for their abilities).

How to solve with 90% chance of success:

Use a specific ability near the end of a powerful attack to ensure you don't fall. Falling is often due to a common bug related to switching back and forth between your initial position and a marked enemy. With any luck near the end of the attack, you might trigger another bug where you'd teleport to your own duplicate. Your duplicates will rarely fall through the floor.

For a specific character: activate one of the abilities, and if the interface indicates an ability is in use, simply roll on the ground and then activate any of the basic abilities again (this is because you cannot roll during any of the animations of those abilities, so you're effectively cancelling the ability in progress). Activating any of the character's abilities would bring out a special weapon allowing you to deactivate it. The game assumes you're still in a powerful mode even though the bug has somehow disarmed you.

I think fighting ability denotes their capability to deal with the number and level of threats. A fully mechanized character can deploy all over a city and handle multiple threats simultaneously, so they score a 10, and another character can obviously influence multiple threats. A score of 9 is probably the maximum for individuals who can't influence entire cities. One character's achievements are based on multiple high-level threats, which is likely why they received a score of 10.

The assessment is suffering from classic data manipulation flaws:

1) They're narrowing the range on the stats (one character counted up to 15, which is a higher range to account for anomalies), so comparisons can't be accurate.

2) The fields are not atomic (if my interpretation of fighting ability is correct, then it can be separated into two more fields: ability to deal with threat level and influence area [speedsters, telekinetics, mechanics would dominate here]). Another example: Endurance/Physical Fitness can be separated into stamina, willpower/pain resistance/tolerance, regeneration, and resistance to damage, classic RPG elements. One character can get a max stat for regeneration and willpower but low for resistance and moderate for stamina (they got exhausted after fighting one high-level threat for 10 minutes).

3) Heterogeneous weighting: from the exams, it seems they make Intelligence and Justice weigh 50% of the exam, while all the other attributes (speed, strength, endurance, fighting ability) account for the other 50%. Instead, if they made all atomic variables weigh equally, the ranking system would be slightly more balanced.

4) They included politics (popularity and achievements).

It's very rare to see an animated series where the main characters aren't the ones who basically dominate the scene.

I do believe those are called fillers... and for some reason, everyone hates them. I remember first watching animated series and never skipping fillers; I actually enjoyed them. Outclassing does not equal scene stealing. A powerful character may outclass everyone, but underpowered characters still manage to steal scenes. This is true for other animated characters like the underdog (everyone loves the underdog... at least he was the underdog).

However, this particular series is different because it cuts everything to the bone; if you remove a scene, there will be diminishment, and if you skip an episode, the whole arc collapses. So instead of filler episodes, there are filler scenes that take up 90% of the show, which is pretty much the same structure as any other series. (I'm not defining fillers as non-canon content, but rather as plot fillers that don't really need filling.)

Almost all popular shows have these side characters going for them; all animated series follow roughly similar character structures:

the rival, the friend from another background with a slight age difference, the brother from another mother without an age difference, the cool character, the angry character, the motivator, the wise old character, the hero, etc.

I would have to disagree and say that the first season of this series is an excellent gateway to animated content, since it's manageable (only 12 episodes), follows roughly the same structure with 90% filler, entertaining fillers (there are quite a few in almost all animated series), same character roles, and a smooth transition from mainstream ensemble shows to character-focused series that also emphasize the background.

The circumference of that band would be the bandwidth (it's the width if you cut the band). So unfortunately, the maximum bandwidth is predetermined by the manufacturer (if it's a rubber band, then the maximum bandwidth is the length at which the rubber snaps).

However, a neat trick to increase your bandwidth is to heat the cable with the constraining object in an oven or with a blowtorch to soften the rubber/plastic, which allows you to increase the maximum stretched length. High noon (aside from references to western movies) is informally represented as a location where the solar noon and the noon of that timezone align. Solar noon varies depending on latitude, and timezones often vary based on longitude. Therefore, high noon refers to a set of small regions. (Although high noon can sometimes refer just to the solar noon if we're not narrowing it down.)

High noon is very difficult to calculate (because date-time data is a mess), and that website is almost certainly off, but if high noon is in a city in Canada, it doesn't matter if you're in another country; it is where it is.
